name: Third Generation 911
tagline: Modernity, all-wheel drive, and the last 911 turbos
description:
When the 964 arrived in late 1988 it looked like a mildly facelifted 911 but was in fact about 85 per cent new, and it quietly introduced features the model line had never had: all-wheel drive, power steering, ABS, an automatically extending rear spoiler, dual ignition with knock control, a three-way catalytic converter and — from 1990 — the Tiptronic automatic gearbox. The drag coefficient fell to 0.32, at the time the most aerodynamic 911 ever built, and coil springs on MacPherson struts front and semi-trailing arms rear replaced the old torsion-bar suspension for the first time in the 911's history.

The engine was the new 3.6-litre M64 flat-six making 250 PS (184 kW) and 310 Nm, with twin-spark ignition technology borrowed from Porsche's aircraft engines. The first car was the 250 PS all-wheel-drive Carrera 4, launched at DM 114,500 in August 1988; the mechanically near-identical rear-wheel-drive Carrera 2 followed a year later from DM 103,500. Coupé, Targa and Cabriolet bodies were all offered, and the 964 Targa was the last 911 built with a genuinely removable roof panel — a layout that would not return until the 991.

The performance arm of the range escalated fast. The 3.3-litre Turbo arrived in 1990 and ran to 3,660 cars, followed by the stripped Turbo S 3.3 Leichtbau, the 55-car Carrera RS 3.8 and its 3.8 RSR race-homologation sibling, the 250-unit America Roadster, the 936-built Speedster and the 911-unit 30th Anniversary Carrera 4. At the very end, around 90 unused Turbo chassis were sent to Porsche Exclusive to be completed by hand as the 385 PS Turbo 3.6 S, 76 of them with the Flachbau slant-nose front end that previewed the 993.

Porsche built 63,762 964s between 1988 and 1994. The generation is now widely regarded as the sweet spot of the air-cooled 911: the last one that still had a removable Targa roof, the last with the upright 1960s-style dash, and the last to be built while the company was still an independent-scale manufacturer rather than a division of a group.

variants.description: The Carrera 4 opened the third generation and was the first series-production 911 with all-wheel drive. Porsche reused the electronically controlled system first developed for the 959 supercar, sending nominally 31 per cent of torque forward and 69 per cent rearward, with a traction-control switch on the centre console. Everything else was new too: coil springs and MacPherson struts up front, semi-trailing arms behind, power steering and ABS, dual ignition, a knock-sensor, a three-way catalyst and a rear spoiler that rose out of the engine lid above 80 km/h and sank flush below that. The 3.6-litre flat-six made 250 PS. It went on sale in August 1988 at DM 114,500 — the first 911 that cost more than 100,000 Deutschmarks — and was the first passenger car fitted with a metal catalytic converter as standard.

variants.description: The rear-wheel-drive Carrera 2 arrived for the 1990 model year, roughly a year after the all-wheel-drive Carrera 4, and Porsche held it back deliberately so the new AWD car would not cannibalise itself. Mechanically it is the same car minus the front differential and driveshaft: same 3.6-litre M64 flat-six at 250 PS and 310 Nm, same coil-sprung suspension, same retractable spoiler, same power steering and ABS. It is also the first 911 offered with the new four-speed Tiptronic automatic, which added 31 kg and cost about 0.9 s over the quarter mile. The saving in weight over the Carrera 4 is around 100 kg DIN, and it is the version most enthusiasts later came to prefer for exactly that reason — the 964 finally steered and rotated with none of the G-series's nervous traits.

variants.description: As the 964 range matured, Porsche began bolting the Turbo's wide bodywork onto the naturally aspirated Carreras. On the all-wheel-drive side this arrived late, as a 1994 model-year wide-body Carrera 4 Coupé, and it is the direct ancestor of the 993 Carrera 4S and the 996 Carrera 4S. The flared Turbo shell gave the car far more visual presence than the narrow 964, and the Turbo-Look package also brought the bigger brakes, stiffer suspension, thicker anti-roll bars and wider wheels and tyres from the 3.3 Turbo, while the normally aspirated 250 PS M64 engine stayed in the back. One North American listing describes such a car as 1 of 267 wide-body coupés ever produced. Note that Porsche never badged a 964 as “Carrera 4S” — the S designation arrived with the 993 in model year 1996.

variants.description: From late 1991 Porsche offered the rear-drive Carrera 2 Coupé and Cabriolet with the Turbo's wide bodywork, badged simply “Turbo-Look”. It was more than a styling exercise: the pack brought the Turbo 3.3's body shell, chassis, braking system and wheels, so the naturally aspirated 250 PS car gained the 322 mm front discs, stiffer springs, thicker anti-roll bars and wider tyres that made the 964 Turbo so good. The narrow-bodied 964 Cabriolet roofline finally matched the beltline, because the arches had grown. Porsche launched three exclusive colours for it — Raspberry Red Metallic, Wimbledon Green Metallic and Lavender Blue Metallic — and in the United States the same car was sold under the America Roadster name. As with the Carrera 4, Porsche never used “Carrera 2S” on a 964; that badge arrived with the 993 Carrera S.

variants.description: Porsche unveiled the 964 Turbo at the 1990 Geneva Motor Show and put it on sale that November, but because there was no time to turbocharge the new 3.6 M64 it simply carried the 930's 3.3-litre engine over, revised to be smoother, freer of turbo lag and stronger at 320 PS and 450 Nm. In exchange, the 964 bodyshell was entirely new: the flared Turbo wings, wider track, deeper front air dam, wider 17-inch wheels, cross-drilled 322 mm front discs and a 36 mm whale-tail wing. It was the last single-turbocharged 911 ever built. The generation's rally-bred suspensions and the standard 964 retractable spoiler made it enormously easier to live with than a 930, and it is the 964 against which every later 911 Turbo is judged — including the one that starred in Bad Boys.

variants.description: The 3.6 Turbo is generally regarded as the finest 911 Porsche ever built before water cooling, and it exists because the Carrera Cup had already proved the M64 durable enough to take boost. Bore and stroke were both increased — 3 mm and 2 mm respectively, adding 300 cc — along with turbo-specific cylinders, pistons and crank train, and compression rose from 7.0 to 7.5:1. Output went to 360 PS and, more importantly, 520 Nm from 4,200 rpm, giving the car a shove that no previous 911 Turbo had. Fewer than 1,500 were built for model years 1993 and 1994, making it one of the rarest Porsches since the 959. A black 1994 car belonged to Michael Bay and starred in the 1995 film Bad Boys.

variants.description: When 964 production ended, roughly 90 unused Turbo chassis remained, and Porsche handed them to Porsche Exclusive to be completed by hand. The result was the Turbo 3.6 S, available with the standard 964 nose or with the famous Flachbau slant-nose option — an X83/X84/X85 package built around the 968 front end, with Exclusive front and rear spoilers and 959-style rear fender intakes, which prefigures the 993. In the US the Flachbau cost $60,179 on top of a $99,000 Turbo 3.6. All 76 slant-nose cars were finished in Polar Silver and split 39 US, 27 international and 10 Japanese. variants.engine: 3.6 L air-cooled flat-six, twin-spark plug ignition, catalytic converter, 11.3:1
variants.transmission: 5-speed manual with modified gear ratios; no power steering
variants.description: The 964 Carrera Cup was the car that made the 964 famous in motorsport and, just as importantly, the direct progenitor of the Carrera RS. Because Porsche judged the newly introduced all-wheel-drive Carrera 4 unsuitable for its own racing series, the Cup was rear-wheel drive only, running from 1990 on a Carrera 2 basis with 265 PS, a welded roll cage, modified chassis set-up, sound deadening deleted, revised gear ratios, no power steering and a 55 mm lower ride height. For 1992 it was substantially revised: RS bodywork, 275 PS, a 20 mm further drop, 18-inch magnesium wheels replacing the aluminium ones, and an ABS that could be switched off for emergency braking or reversing. Retaining a catalyst and ABS was unusual for a race car of the period and reflected the regulations the series had to satisfy.

Contemporary cars are now extraordinarily valuable and the model is effectively unobtainable.

variants.description: The Turbo S LM-GT was Porsche's 1993 assault on GT racing, started from a road-legal 964 Turbo S and stripped for the circuit: a deep chin spoiler, two air inlets above the rear arches, an adjustable racing wing on top of the standard wing, and widened arches for 12-inch slicks. Inside were a roll cage, plastic windows and no trim. Crucially the engine was not the road unit but a 3.2-litre twin-turbo making 475 hp. The Brumos entry of Röhrl, Stuck and Haywood finished seventh overall and first in class at the 1993 12 Hours of Sebring, then ran as a works car at Le Mans before failing. For 1994 it went to Larbre Compétition with a 993-based 3.6 twin-turbo, winning the 24 Hours of Daytona and four BPR Global GT races. The programme fed directly into the 993 GT2.
